title: One Region, Five Workforces: Why a Single Southeast Asia Engagement Strategy Fails
summary: Engagement in Southeast Asia ranges from 39% in the Philippines to 14% in Singapore. Why one regional strategy fails, and what to do instead.
body_markdown:
Most multinationals manage Southeast Asia as one region. One engagement survey, one benchmark, one action plan, usually designed at a regional headquarters in Singapore and rolled out everywhere else.


It's efficient. It's also a reliable way to misread your own people.


The latest data shows that "Southeast Asia" is not one workforce. It's at least five, each with a different problem. A strategy built for the regional average fits none of them.


## The average hides five different workforces


Gallup puts Southeast Asia's engagement average at 25%, above the global 20%. Here's what that average is made of:


Country


Employees engaged at work


Philippines


39%


Thailand


34%


Indonesia


27%


Malaysia


25%


Singapore


14%


That's a 25-point spread inside a single region. Stress varies just as widely: 50% of Filipino employees reported a lot of stress the previous day, against 43% in Singapore, 25% in Thailand and just 14% in Indonesia.


If your regional dashboard shows one number, it is showing you a fiction.


## Same region, different problems


**Philippines: engaged, but burning out.** The most engaged workforce in the region is also the most stressed. With 76% of employees saying it's a good time to find a job, the risk is high performers burning out and getting hired away.


**Singapore: disengaged, but staying.** Engagement is the lowest in the region and has barely moved since 2019. Only 42% think it's a good time to find a job, so disengaged employees stay put. The risk is quiet, invisible productivity loss.


**Indonesia: calm, but uneasy about AI.** Indonesian employees report the lowest daily stress in the region. Yet 61% rank over-dependence on AI as a top concern, the highest of six markets in a Milieu Insight study. The risk is a poorly handled AI rollout.


**Thailand: wellbeing as a currency.** Daily stress in Thailand has fallen sharply, from 41% to 25%. And 56% of Thai employees say they would take a pay cut for better wellbeing benefits. Wellbeing is a retention lever here in a way it isn't everywhere.


**Malaysia: adopting AI faster than people are comfortable with.** Malaysia's score on the WiN World AI Index rose from 60.5 to 67.4 this year, but its comfort score fell from 42.5 to 38.7. Adoption is outpacing trust.


Five countries. Five different headlines. One regional action plan cannot answer all of them.


## Where regional programmes go wrong


**One benchmark.** Compare your Manila team to the regional average and they look outstanding, right up until they resign from exhaustion. Compare your Singapore team to the same average and they look like a failure, no matter what their managers do.


**One language.** An English-only survey works in Singapore. In Jakarta, Bangkok or Ho Chi Minh City, it filters out the employees who would be most honest in their own language, often the frontline and operations staff you most need to hear from.


**One action plan.** When regional HQ decides the top three priorities for every country, local HR teams end up running initiatives that solve someone else's problem.


**One annual cycle.** Five workforces moving at five different speeds won't wait for a once-a-year survey to catch up.


## A better model: shared core, local drivers


You don't need five separate programmes. You need one structure that respects the differences.


**1. Keep a common core.** A small set of questions asked everywhere gives leadership a consistent view across the region.


**2. Benchmark each country against itself.** Track how each country moves over time and against its own local market, not against a regional average that describes nowhere.


**3. Add local drivers.** Ask Filipino teams about workload and recovery. Ask Singapore teams about career progression. Ask Indonesian and Malaysian teams about AI and change. Let each country add what matters there.


**4. Listen in local languages.** Bahasa Indonesia, Bahasa Melayu, Thai, Vietnamese and Filipino. The cost of translation is tiny next to the cost of missing the truth.


**5. Give country leaders ownership of the actions.** Regional HQ should set the standard and track progress. Country HR leaders should decide what to fix first.


## The bottom line


Southeast Asia is one of the most exciting talent markets in the world precisely because it is so varied. Treating it as one workforce wastes that. The organisations that win here will be the ones that can see five different stories and respond to each.
